newsitem.title: USA: Study finds loners get more colds.
newsitem.headline: Study finds loners get more colds.

text.p: Social butterflies get fewer colds than loners, researchers reported on Tuesday, perhaps because being active and needed improves immune responses.

Having friends, neighbours -- even a boss -- helps people resist colds, according to psychologist Sheldon Cohen of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, whose landmark 1991 study linked stress to the common cold, and colleagues.
In the new study published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association, common cold viruses were sprayed into the noses of 276 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 55.

Of those who had three or fewer roles or relationships, 62 percent came down with a cold. But only 43 percent of those with four or five kinds of social relationships and 35 percent of those with six or more types of relationships got colds.

"Those with more types of relationships were more resistant to upper respiratory illness. Having many types of relationships was more important than the sheer number of people in their social networks," Cohen said.

Those in the study were measured against 12 possible relationships including being a spouse, a parent, a child, a parent-in-law, a close family member or neighbour, a friend, a classmate, a church or club member or an employee.

Exactly why being social protects against the common cold is a mystery, the study said. One possibility was that people with diverse relationships are motivated to take better care of themselves because their contacts promote feelings of self-worth, responsibility, control and meaning in life.

But Cohen said the study found that good health practices were apparently only a small factor in the cold resistance effect turned up by the study. He also said the study found no direct evidence such contacts alter moods and cause changes in the levels of hormones that help regulate immune systems.
Cohen nontheless speculated that "differences in immume response were probably responsible" for the variations in susceptibility to colds found in his study.

"Among healthy humans, it is difficult to accurately characterise the readiness of the immune system to fight infections, making a demonstration of the importance of immunity in this process a challenge," he said. But he added: "Telling people to reduce stress and enjoy the support of their friends, family and their peers is never a bad thing."
Previous research has shown that people with multiple ties to family and community tend to live longer.
